newsitem.title: FRANCE: British beef embargo to stay, says EU.
newsitem.headline: British beef embargo to stay, says EU.

text.p: The European Union said on Thursday it would maintain an embargo on British beef exports after scientists found more evidence that mad cow disease could spread to people.
"What the British scientists have discovered shows how serious the crisis is," EU Agriculture Commissioner Franz Fischler told a news conference in Paris.
"We must make sure all the measures which have been put in place are maintained, because now we have to face the fact that the disease can be transmitted to people," he said.

The research published on Wednesday found that a new variant of fatal Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) in humans left traces very similar to brain-wasting mad cow disease -- bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE).

The research "shows that the risk of transmission to humans is a fact -- it is not the proof, but it is one more proof," Fischler said after briefing a French parliamentary committee on the seven-month-old European beef crisis.
Speaking in German through a French translator, the Austrian commissioner said the evidence reinforced the need for an eradication plan agreed by EU leaders this summer to be fully implemented.
"It demonstrates that the measures agreed between Britain and other states must be maintained," Fischler said.
The EU banned British beef exports in March after London first reported a suspected link between mad cow disease and CJD.
At a summit in June, EU leaders agreed on a series of steps Britain must take to get the global export ban lifted, including an accelerated slaughter programme of 147,000 cattle.
But London put the additional cull on hold last month after experts said it would not speed up the disappearance of BSE.
Fischler said the cull was a pre-condition for the export ban to be eased.

France, the first country to ban imports of British beef when the crisis broke, said the new evidence justified its crackdown. It said French health controls were the toughest in the European Union and urged EU nations to harmonise regulations.

"There is a lot left to do since the crisis is not over," Agriculture Minister Philippe Vasseur told the National Assembly, noting that France had stepped up financial support for beef producers after consumption slumped.
British Prime Minister John Major insisted earlier on Thursday that meat from British cattle was safe to eat despite the latest findings.
He said there was no justification for the EU to harden its stance against lifting the export ban.
